In casual talk people often say someone is 'a Renaissance man' or 'really well-rounded.' Calling someone a polymath may sound overly formal or like flattery if they are not known for range.

distinctions.note: An expert is deep in one field, while a polymath is broadly knowledgeable across many fields.
Generalist can be neutral or slightly negative, while polymath is a stronger, more admiring term.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a polymath who can fix a car, bake bread, and explain the stock market.
examples.professional: Our team lead is a polymath who understands statistics, software design, and the business side of the product.
examples.analytical: Leonardo is often called a polymath, but his breadth also depended on the patronage and interdisciplinary culture of his age.

nuance.analogy: A polymath is like a skilled traveler who knows many roads and can reach any destination by a different route.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polymathēs, having learned much, from polys, many, and manthanein, to learn.
common_mistakes: Using polymath to describe someone who is only good at two related subjects
Saying 'polymathic person' when 'polymath' alone is more natural

polymath.etymology: Ancient Greek *πολυμαθής* (“having learnt much”), first attested in 1624.

senses.definition: The quality of a text of being able to be read in more than one way.
senses.example: the polyphony of a biblical passage

senses.definition: Musical texture consisting of several independent melodic voices, as opposed to music with just one voice (monophony) or music with one dominant melodic voice accompanied by chords (homophony).

core.definition: Music in which two or more independent melodic lines sound together, or a text that supports several equal voices or readings.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, LIF, with a short i like in sit. The unstressed endings reduce to uh and nee, so avoid saying the final syllable as a long ee sound with extra emphasis.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests richness and complexity in music or writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use polyphony mainly in music history, music theory, and literary criticism. In music, it often contrasts with homophony, where one melody is supported by chords. People outside those fields may use it loosely to describe a rich mix of voices in a novel or a city, but it sounds slightly academic in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Homophony has one melody with chordal accompaniment, while polyphony has several melodies that move independently.
Harmony refers to the vertical sound of chords; polyphony refers to the horizontal independence of separate melodic lines.
Monophony is a single melodic line with no accompaniment, which is the opposite texture of polyphony.

examples.everyday: My choir director said Bach's motets are a great example of polyphony, with every voice singing its own line.
examples.professional: For the music department grant, we need a short description of how polyphony shapes the texture of the mass.
examples.analytical: Bakhtin's notion of polyphony in Dostoevsky describes a narrative where characters' voices remain independent rather than subordinated to the author's judgment.

nuance.analogy: Polyphony is like a group of friends each telling their own story at the same table, so you follow several threads at once instead of one speaker.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polyphōnia, 'many sounds', from poly- 'many' and phōnē 'sound, voice'.
common_mistakes: Confusing polyphony with polyphonic ringtones or phone sounds, which is a different meaning.
Using polyphony as a count noun, as in a polyphony, when the word is normally used as a mass noun.

senses.definition: Something assumed without proof as being self-evident or generally accepted, especially when used as a basis for an argument. Sometimes distinguished from axioms as being relevant to a particular science or context, rather than universally true, and following from other axioms rather than being an absolute assumption.
A fundamental element; a basic principle.
An axiom.
A requirement; a prerequisite.
To assume as a truthful or accurate premise or axiom, especially as a basis of an argument.
(historical) To appoint or request one's appointment to an ecclesiastical office.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A statement assumed to be true without proof and used as the starting point for an argument, theory or proof.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like PAHS-chuh-let, not pos-TYOO-late. The verb is different: PAHS-chuh-late, with a long a at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a logical starting point and carries no judgment about whether the assumption is true.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use postulate mostly in math, science, philosophy and formal argument, for example when someone says a model rests on certain postulates. In everyday talk people say assumption or premise instead. In the US the word can also appear in Catholic contexts, where a postulate is a candidate for a religious order, but that sense is rare outside church life.

distinctions.note: An axiom is usually treated as self-evident and universal, while a postulate is often a working assumption specific to one theory or field.
A hypothesis is a testable claim you expect to confirm or reject, while a postulate is accepted as a foundation and is not tested in the same way.
Assumption is the everyday word for any unstated belief; postulate is more formal and is used when the assumption is stated explicitly as a basis for reasoning.

examples.everyday: My brother's whole argument about the car rests on the postulate that newer cars never break down, which is not true.
examples.professional: Before we build the forecasting model, we need to agree on the postulate that customer demand is stable across quarters.
examples.analytical: Descartes takes as a postulate the existence of a thinking subject, and the rest of his method is built on that starting point.

nuance.analogy: A postulate is like the foundation slab of a house: you pour it first and do not dig it up to check every time you add a room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin postulatum, 'something demanded,' from postulare, 'to demand.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in pos-TOO-late, instead of PAHS-chuh-let.
Using postulate as a verb in everyday speech when assume or suppose is more natural.
Confusing the noun postulate with the verb postulate, which is pronounced with a long a at the end.

senses.definition: To make something happen suddenly and quickly.
senses.example: to precipitate a journey, or a conflict

senses.definition: To throw an object or person from a great height.
To send violently into a certain state or condition.
senses.example: we were precipitated into a conflict

senses.definition: To have water in the air fall to the ground, for example as rain, snow, sleet, or hail; be deposited as condensed droplets.
senses.example: It will precipitate tomorrow, but we don't know whether as rain or snow.

senses.definition: To cause (water in the air) to condense or fall to the ground.
To fall headlong.
To act too hastily; to be precipitous.
(chemistry) To come out of a liquid solution into solid form.
senses.example: Adding the acid will cause the salt to precipitate.

senses.definition: (chemistry) To separate a substance out of a liquid solution into solid form.
Headlong; falling steeply or vertically.
Very steep; precipitous.
With a hasty impulse; hurried; headstrong.
Moving with excessive speed or haste; overly hasty.
senses.example: The king was too precipitate in declaring war.

senses.definition: Performed very rapidly or abruptly.
A product resulting from a process, event, or course of action.
A solid that exits the liquid phase of a solution.

core.definition: To cause something, often something bad, to happen suddenly or sooner than expected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the second syllable, SIP. The first syllable is a reduced 'pri', and the verb ends in 'ayt', while the adjective and noun are pronounced with 'it'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it usually describes bad events or sudden worsening.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use precipitate in news, politics, and business writing for events that suddenly trigger a crisis, as in 'the scandal precipitated his resignation'. In casual talk, people say set off, bring on, or cause. Use it as a verb, and remember to pronounce the final 'ayt' clearly.

distinctions.note: Cause is neutral and everyday, while precipitate suggests a sudden, often dramatic trigger.
Trigger is informal and common, while precipitate is more formal and usually describes crises.

examples.everyday: One rude comment from my uncle precipitated a long argument at dinner.
examples.professional: A sudden outage in the database precipitated an urgent rollback of the release.
examples.analytical: Rising inequality may precipitate political instability, though the causal link remains contested among historians.

nuance.analogy: Like a single spark that sets dry grass on fire.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praecipitare, 'to throw headlong', from praeceps, 'headlong'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the verb with the adjective precipitate, which is pronounced with a final 'it'.
Dropping the final syllable in speech, so it sounds like 'pri-SIP-iht'.

precipitate.etymology: From Latin *praecipitātus*, perfect passive participle of *praecipitō* (“throw down, hurl down, throw headlong”) (see *-ate* for more), from *praeceps* (“head foremost, headlong”), from *prae* + *-ceps*.

senses.definition: To prevent, to make impossible.
To remove the possibility from consideration; to rule out or exclude.
senses.example: It has been raining for days, but that doesn’t preclude the skies clearing by this afternoon!

senses.definition: To ban.
To prevent by mutual exclusion; where one thing prevents another because they are mutually exclusive.

core.definition: To make something impossible or unlikely by acting in advance; to rule out a possibility.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -CLUDE, which rhymes with 'rude'. Keep the first vowel short and relaxed, not 'pree'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a logical or practical effect rather than an emotion, so it fits discussions of rules, options and outcomes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'preclude' mostly in writing, meetings, policy discussions and legal or technical contexts. In casual talk they would say 'rule out' or 'keep you from'. It is usually followed by a noun or -ing form, as in 'This does not preclude further testing.'

distinctions.note: 'Prevent' is everyday and direct; 'preclude' is more formal and often implies that the option is removed in advance, not that an action is stopped.
'Exclude' means leaving something out of a group or set; 'preclude' means making something impossible or ruling it out as a possibility.

examples.everyday: Your work schedule doesn't preclude us from getting dinner, so let's just pick a night.
examples.professional: The vendor's contract clause does not preclude us from switching providers next quarter, but it does require 60 days' notice.
examples.analytical: The strong form of determinism would preclude genuine moral responsibility, which is why compatibilists redefine freedom.

nuance.analogy: A locked gate at the trailhead: it doesn't stop you from wanting to hike, it simply takes that route off the table.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praecludere, 'to close off in advance', from prae- 'before' and claudere 'to shut'.
common_mistakes: Using 'preclude' for a simple stop, as in 'The rain precluded me from leaving'. Americans would more naturally say 'prevented' in casual speech.
Pronouncing it 'pre-KLUDE' with a long first vowel; the first syllable is 'prih'.

senses.definition: A term of a statement, where the statement may be true or false depending on whether the thing referred to by the values of the statement's variables has the property signified by that (predicative) term.
senses.example: A propositional variable may be treated as a nullary predicate.

senses.definition: The part of the sentence (or clause) which states a property that a subject has or is characterized by.
An operator, expression, or function that returns either true or false.
To assert or state as an attribute or quality of something.
To announce, assert, or proclaim publicly.
To assume or suppose; to infer.
To base (on); to assert on the grounds of.
To make a term (or expression) the predicate of a statement.
Of or related to the predicate of a sentence or clause.
Predicated, stated.
Relating to or being any of a series of criminal acts upon which prosecution for racketeering may be predicated.

core.definition: The part of a sentence that says something about the subject, usually including the verb and what follows it.

pronunciation.tip: The noun is stressed on the first syllable and ends in 'it,' while the verb is PRED-ih-kayt. Many learners pronounce the noun ending as 'kate,' so listen for the reduced final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use predicate mainly in grammar, logic, computing and law. In a school setting, a teacher might ask students to identify the subject and predicate. In everyday talk it almost never comes up, and people would say 'the verb part' or 'what it says about the subject.'

distinctions.note: The subject is the person or thing the sentence is about, while the predicate is what is said about it.
The predicate is the whole part after the subject, while the predicate verb is only the main verb within it.

examples.everyday: My daughter's homework asked her to underline the subject and circle the predicate.
examples.professional: In the schema, each rule has a predicate that returns true or false based on the input record.
examples.analytical: Frege treated the predicate as a function that maps objects to truth values, a view that transformed modern logic.

nuance.analogy: If the subject is the star of a sentence, the predicate is the story told about the star.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praedicatum, from praedicare, 'to proclaim or assert.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the noun as PRED-ih-kate, which is the verb pronunciation.
Confusing predicate with predicament, which is a difficult situation.
Using predicate to mean a prediction, which is not its meaning.

predicate.etymology: From Middle English *predicat*, from Old French *predicat*, from Medieval Latin *praedicātum* (“thing said of a subject, predicate”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of *praedicātus*, the perfect passive participle *praedicō* (“to…

senses.definition: Acting in advance to deal with an expected change or difficulty.
senses.example: We can deal with each problem as it pops up, or we can take a proactive stance and try to prevent future problems.

core.definition: Taking action early to prevent a problem or to prepare for a change, rather than waiting until it happens.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable, 'AK', like 'act'. Do not stress the first syllable, and keep the final 'ive' short, like 'tiv'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises initiative and foresight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'proactive' a lot in workplace settings, performance reviews and job interviews, often as a compliment. You might hear 'Let's be proactive about this' in a meeting. The opposite, waiting for things to happen, is usually called 'reactive', which can sound critical.

distinctions.note: 'Preventive' focuses on stopping a specific problem from happening, while 'proactive' emphasizes taking initiative in general, including seeking opportunities.
'Active' only means doing something, while 'proactive' means acting first, before a problem or event forces you to.

examples.everyday: My mom is proactive about her health, so she gets a checkup every year.
examples.professional: I'd like us to be proactive and send the client an update before they ask for one.
examples.analytical: A proactive ethic asks not only how one responds to harm, but how one anticipates and shapes the conditions that produce it.

nuance.analogy: Being proactive is like fixing a leaky roof before the next storm, instead of mopping up after the ceiling falls in.
nuance.etymology: From pro- 'forward, before' plus 'active', from Latin agere 'to do'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'proactive' with 'reactive', which means the opposite.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'PRO-active', which sounds unnatural.

proactive.etymology: From *pro* + *active*; originally coined 1933 by Paul Whiteley and Gerald Blankfort in a psychology paper, used in technical sense.

senses.definition: Reasoning under uncertainty using probabilities.

core.definition: Reasoning under uncertainty by weighing the probabilities of possible outcomes and updating beliefs as new evidence arrives.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'LIS' in the first word and 'REE' in the second. The 'z' in 'reasoning' is voiced, and the final 'ing' is a light nasal, not a hard 'ink'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical phrase.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in artificial intelligence, decision science and philosophy of science to describe systems that reason with uncertain information. It is not usually a casual phrase, but you might hear it in a tech meeting or a university lecture. In conversation, people often say 'reasoning with probabilities' or 'thinking in odds' instead.

distinctions.note: Deductive reasoning draws certain conclusions from premises, while probabilistic reasoning concludes only that something is likely.
Statistical inference draws conclusions about a population from data, while probabilistic reasoning is a broader way of reasoning about beliefs and decisions.

examples.everyday: I can't be sure the bus will be on time, but I use probabilistic reasoning and leave early just in case.
examples.professional: Our fraud model uses probabilistic reasoning to score each transaction, so the team can set thresholds for review.
examples.analytical: Probabilistic reasoning allows an agent to revise its beliefs gradually as new evidence arrives, rather than holding them as fixed truths.

nuance.analogy: Probabilistic reasoning is like a sailor reading the wind and waves: no certainty about the next wave, but a careful judgment of what is likely.
nuance.etymology: Probabilistic from probability (Latin probabilis, 'provable, credible') plus -istic, and reasoning from reason (Latin ratio).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in 'probabilistic', as in 'prah-buh-BIL-is-tik'.
Treating probabilistic reasoning as meaning 'guessing', when it means calculating likelihoods carefully.

conversation.text: Probabilistic reasoning updates beliefs as evidence arrives instead of treating facts as simply true or false.
Sensor data is noisy, so the robot relies on probabilistic reasoning to estimate where it is.

senses.definition: The assignment of something to a period of time that precedes it.
The anticipation of an objection to an argument.
A construction that consists of placing an element in a syntactic unit before that to which it would logically correspond.
A so-called "preconception", i.e. a pre-theoretical notion which can lead to true knowledge of the world.
The practice of placing information about the ending of a story near the beginning, as a literary device.
Growth in which lateral branches develop from a lateral meristem, after the formation of a bud or following a period of dormancy, when the lateral meristem is split from a terminal meristem.

core.definition: The answering of an objection or the treatment of a future event as if it had already happened, used in rhetoric and narrative.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, LEP, and the first vowel is a long OH. Don't add an extra vowel between the p and s in the middle cluster, and make the final syllable short and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term from rhetoric, grammar and narratology, so it describes a device rather than carrying praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in English classes, literary criticism, rhetoric and linguistics. It is not used in casual talk. In a literature seminar you might hear 'the novel uses prolepsis to hint at the ending.' Most people would say 'anticipating an objection' instead.

distinctions.note: Foreshadowing is a general hint of what is to come, while prolepsis is the specific device of narrating or referring to a future event before it happens.
Analepsis, also called flashback, moves backward in time, while prolepsis moves forward.

examples.everyday: Our book club leader said the opening chapter was a prolepsis, because it showed the ending first.
examples.professional: In the grant proposal, we used prolepsis by describing the final results before explaining the method.
examples.analytical: The author's prolepsis in the first chapter forecasts the father's death, which shapes how the reader interprets every later scene.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie trailer that shows the ending before the story has started, prolepsis shows a future event before the text reaches it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek prólēpsis, 'anticipation', from pro- 'before' and lambánein 'to take'.
common_mistakes: Confusing prolepsis with prologue, which is an introduction to a story or play.
Stressing the wrong syllable as PRO-lep-sis instead of pro-LEP-sis.

prolepsis.etymology: From Latin *prolepsis*, from Ancient Greek *πρόληψις* (“preconception, anticipation”), from *προλαμβάνω* (“take beforehand, anticipate”).

senses.definition: To seek to obtain by legal process.
senses.example: to prosecute a right or a claim in a court of law

senses.definition: To pursue something to the end.
senses.example: to prosecute a scheme, hope, or an investigation

senses.definition: To start criminal proceedings against.
senses.example: to prosecute a man for trespass, or for a riot

senses.definition: To charge, try.

core.definition: To bring criminal charges against someone and pursue them in court on behalf of the government.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PRAH. The second syllable is a reduced 'suh,' and the final part is 'kyoot' with a long oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a legal action, though it can sound serious or aggressive depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prosecute mostly in legal news and everyday talk about crime, as in 'The district attorney will prosecute the case.' In casual speech, people might say 'press charges' when a victim takes action. The word is not used for personal disputes, which would be 'sue.'

distinctions.note: Persecute means to treat someone cruelly or unjustly over time, especially for beliefs, while prosecute means to bring a legal case in court.
Sue means to bring a civil lawsuit, usually for money or damages, while prosecute refers to criminal charges brought by the government.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the city will prosecute anyone caught dumping trash illegally by the river.
examples.professional: Legal will prosecute the vendor for breach of contract if they fail to deliver by Friday.
examples.analytical: Whether a state should prosecute such crimes in federal or local courts is largely a question of jurisdiction.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach pushing a team to the finish line, carrying the case all the way through court.
nuance.etymology: From Latin prosequi, meaning 'to follow up' or 'to pursue.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'persecute,' which has a very different meaning about cruel treatment.
Saying 'prosecute him of the crime'; the correct form is 'prosecute him for the crime.'

prosecute.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *prōsecūtus*, perfect participle of *prōsequor*. from Old French.

senses.definition: A system or policy of protecting the domestic producers of a product from foreign competition by imposing tariffs, quotas, duties or other barriers on importations.
Linguistic purism.

core.definition: Government policy that protects domestic industries from foreign competition through tariffs, quotas or other trade barriers.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TEK. Reduce the first vowel to uh and say the -tion as shun, and keep the final -ism light, not a full ism.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economics, but often negative in political debate, where critics link it to higher prices and trade wars.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use protectionism in economics, politics and business news, especially in debates about tariffs and trade with China or other countries. Supporters may call it defending American jobs, while critics call it a trade war policy. It is not used for personal protection of people, which would be expressed differently.

distinctions.note: Free trade means reducing or removing trade barriers; protectionism is the opposite policy of raising barriers to protect domestic producers.
Isolationism refers to avoiding foreign political or military involvement; protectionism concerns trade and tariffs specifically.

examples.everyday: My uncle is always complaining about protectionism and says it raises the price of everything at the store.
examples.professional: The supply chain report warns that rising protectionism could add tariffs to our imported components next year.
examples.analytical: Protectionism assumes that national wealth is best guarded by walls, yet it often shifts costs onto consumers and trade partners.

nuance.analogy: Protectionism is like putting a fence around a garden: it keeps out pests, but it also keeps out the bees that help the plants grow.
nuance.etymology: From protection, from Latin protegere, to cover in front, plus -ism.
common_mistakes: Using protectionism for personal safety, when it refers to trade policy only.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying pruh-tek-SHUN-iz-um.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to protectionism, or an advocate thereof.
Someone who believes in protecting domestic producers by impeding or limiting the importation of foreign goods and services via actions taken by government.
A linguistic purist.

core.definition: A person who supports government policies that protect domestic industries from foreign competition through trade barriers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEK, and the -tion ending is shun. Many learners insert an extra vowel before the -ist, so keep it short and clipped.

nuance.connotation: Often negative in economic debate, since critics see it as protecting special interests; supporters use it with pride.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use protectionist in politics and business news, often as a label that critics put on opponents of free trade. Supporters may describe themselves as pro-American-jobs instead. As an adjective it describes policies, such as protectionist tariffs.

distinctions.note: A free trader supports open markets with few trade barriers, the opposite view.
Nationalist is broader and can refer to political identity; protectionist refers specifically to trade policy.

examples.everyday: My neighbor calls himself a protectionist because he wants to buy American, even if it costs more.
examples.professional: Our procurement team is wary of the protectionist senator who wants to block the vendor.
examples.analytical: The protectionist argument often treats domestic employment as a fixed pie, which economists dispute.

nuance.analogy: A protectionist is like a gatekeeper who checks every visitor at the door, even when the visitors bring things the house needs.
nuance.etymology: From protection plus -ist, from Latin protegere, to cover in front.
common_mistakes: Using protectionist for someone who protects people physically, such as a bodyguard.
Confusing the noun protectionist with the adjective form when describing policies.

senses.definition: A flaw in a system or process whereby the output or result is unexpectedly and critically dependent on the sequence or timing of other events.
senses.example: A race condition in writing my guest book file meant that the last person to sign wiped out all previous signatures.

core.definition: A bug in a program or system where the result depends on the unpredictable timing or order of concurrent events.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, DISH, and keep the first word's main stress light. The "-tion" ending is "shun," and "condition" is reduced to "kun-DISH-un" in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it describes a bug, not a judgment of people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use race condition mainly in software engineering, operating systems, and distributed systems. It usually appears in code reviews, bug reports, and design discussions. In casual talk the phrase would be confusing, since "race" can also mean ethnicity, so keep it in technical contexts.

distinctions.note: A race condition produces wrong results from unpredictable timing, while a deadlock occurs when threads wait on each other forever.
Bug is a general term for any defect; race condition specifies a timing-dependent error in concurrent code.

examples.everyday: My laptop kept crashing randomly, and my friend said it was probably a race condition in the software.
examples.professional: The test failures are intermittent because of a race condition between the two workers writing to the same database row.
examples.analytical: A race condition arises when correctness depends on the interleaving of operations that the programmer did not explicitly synchronize, so the program's output is not a function of its inputs alone.

nuance.analogy: A race condition is like two people trying to sign the same check at once: whose signature lands first changes the outcome.
common_mistakes: Confusing race condition with the social meaning of race in everyday talk.
Stressing both words equally instead of putting the main stress on the second word.

senses.definition: The state of being recalcitrant.

core.definition: Stubborn refusal to obey, cooperate, or accept correction, especially when someone keeps resisting despite pressure.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on KAL, the second syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, so the 'i' sounds like a quick 'ih', and the final -ance is a weak 'uhns'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes stubbornness that is frustrating or obstructive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use recalcitrance in writing, news, and formal speech about people, institutions, or systems that resist change. In casual talk people usually say 'stubbornness' or 'resistance', so recalcitrance can sound a bit bookish at a dinner table. It works well in an article or a thoughtful workplace discussion.

distinctions.note: Stubbornness is the common everyday word; recalcitrance is more formal and often implies resistance to authority or to a required process.
Obstinacy is stubbornness of opinion or purpose; recalcitrance more often describes refusal to comply with rules or pressure.
Defiance is open, active disobedience; recalcitrance can be quieter, a persistent refusal to move.

examples.everyday: My dad's recalcitrance about using his phone for directions drives my sister crazy.
examples.professional: The vendor's recalcitrance about the contract terms delayed our launch by three weeks.
examples.analytical: Her argument turns on the recalcitrance of institutions, which resist reform even when the evidence for change is overwhelming.

nuance.analogy: Recalcitrance is like a mule that plants its feet and will not move, no matter how hard you pull the rope.
nuance.etymology: From Latin recalcitrare, 'to kick back', from re- 'back' and calx 'heel'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as re-KAL-sih-trunce; the stress belongs on KAL.
Using it for a simple lack of skill or ability; it refers to willful resistance.

recalcitrance.etymology: In use since at least 1856 (Webster's Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary, published 1985).

senses.definition: The end of estrangement between a human and God as a result of atonement.
The reconsecration of a desecrated church or other holy site.
Admission of a person to membership of the church, or readmission after the person has previously left the church.
The re-establishment of friendly relations; conciliation, rapprochement.
senses.example: He longed for reconciliation with his estranged father, but painful memories made him feel unready to do so.

senses.definition: The process of comparing and resolving apparent differences between sets of accounting records, or between accounting records and bank statements, receipts, etc.
Religious senses.

Ellipsis of sacrament of reconciliation (“a sacrament (sacred ritual) also called confession, involving contrition by a person, confessing sins to a priest, penance performed by the person, and absolution granted by the priest”).
A special parliamentary procedure of the United States Congress to expedite the passage of certain federal budget legislation in the Senate, overriding the Senate's filibuster rules.

core.definition: The restoration of friendly relations after conflict; in theology, the ending of estrangement between humans and God through Christ.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on 'AY'. There are five syllables, with secondary stress on the first and third. Reduce the second syllable to a schwa, and don't say 'recon-SILE'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it implies healing and restored relationship. In accounting, it is neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'reconciliation' for repairing relationships, in politics (truth and reconciliation), in budgeting (a legislative process), and in accounting (bank reconciliation). In church life it can refer to the Catholic sacrament, also called confession. In everyday talk, people more often say 'make up' or 'patch things up'.

distinctions.note: Forgiveness is releasing a wrong; reconciliation restores the relationship and takes two parties.
Atonement is the act that makes amends for sin; reconciliation is the resulting restored relationship.
Reunion is simply coming together again, without the sense of resolving conflict.

examples.everyday: After years of not talking, my dad and his brother finally had a reconciliation at the family reunion.
examples.professional: Finance will complete the monthly account reconciliation before we close the books on Friday.
examples.analytical: Paul describes the cross as God's initiative in reconciliation, so that the estrangement caused by sin is overcome from God's side.

nuance.analogy: Like rebuilding a bridge across a river that had divided two towns.
nuance.etymology: From Latin reconciliatio, from reconciliare, 'to make friendly again.'
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the wrong syllable, such as recon-SIL-iation.
Using 'reconciliation' when 'reconcile' (verb) is needed.
Saying 'reconciliation to someone' instead of 'reconciliation with someone'.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek katallagē ('exchange, reconciliation') and katallassō ('to reconcile') describe restored relationship. Romans 5:10 says we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son while we were enemies. 2 Corinthians 5:18-20 calls believers ambassadors entrusted with the ministry of reconciliation. Colossians 1:20 says God reconciles all things to himself through Christ.

traditions.view: Reconciliation with God and the Church is received in the mystery of confession (repentance), where the penitent is absolved by a priest and restored to communion.
Reconciliation is a sacrament, also called penance or confession, in which a priest gives absolution to the repentant, restoring friendship with God and the Church.

Most Protestants treat reconciliation as accomplished by Christ's work and received by faith, without a sacrament of penance. Lutherans and Anglicans retain optional private confession, while Baptists and others emphasize direct confession to God.

senses.definition: An improvement (or an intended improvement) in the existing form or condition of institutions or practices, etc. intended to make a striking change for the better in social, political or religious affairs or in the conduct of persons or operation of organizations.
Change or correction, by a court in equity, to a written instrument to conform to the original intention of the parties.

core.definition: A major change to improve a religious, social or political institution, especially the sixteenth-century break from Rome that created Protestant churches.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'MAY', and the 'er' in the second syllable is a quick American r-colored vowel. Don't say 'ref-or-MAY-shun' with a full 'or' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most contexts, since reform implies improvement; in theology it can be contested, depending on whether one sees the change as legitimate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans capitalize 'Reformation' when referring to the 16th-century movement led by Luther, Calvin and Zwingli. In general talk, 'reform' or 'overhaul' is often more natural for a change to a system. Saying 'the Reformation' alone usually refers to the religious event, and context signals which sense is meant.

distinctions.note: Reform is the action or process; reformation is the result or the named historical movement. The word is more formal and often used for large-scale change.
A revival restores existing religious fervor, while a reformation changes doctrine, practice or institutions.

examples.everyday: My uncle loves history books about the Reformation, so we talk about Luther every holiday.
examples.professional: The nonprofit plans a reformation of its grant process to cut approval times in half.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the Reformation was primarily a theological reformation or a political and social upheaval.

nuance.analogy: A reformation is like renovating a house from the foundation up, not just repainting one room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin reformatio, a re-forming or restoring, from reformare, to form again.
common_mistakes: Using 'reformation' for small everyday fixes; 'reform' or 'improvement' fits better.
Forgetting the capital R when referring to the historical movement.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church sees the sixteenth-century Reformation as a schism that departed from the continuous tradition of the undivided Church, not as a return to the apostolic faith.
The Catholic Church views the Reformation as a rupture with papal authority and doctrine, while acknowledging that the Council of Trent carried out internal reforms in response.
Protestants generally regard the Reformation as a necessary recovery of biblical truth, though Lutherans, Reformed and Anglicans differ on its scope and aims.

reformation.etymology: From Middle English *reformacioun*, *reformation*, from Middle French *reformation* and Latin *reformatio* (“reform, change”), from *refōrmō* (“transform, reshape”), from *re-* + *fōrmō* (“shape, form”).

senses.definition: To renew or revitalize.
senses.example: Sleep refreshes the body and the mind.

senses.definition: To become fresh again; to be revitalized.
To reload (a document, especially a webpage) and show any new changes.
To cause (a web browser or similar software) to refresh its display.
To perform the periodic energizing required to maintain the contents of computer memory, the display luminance of a computer screen, etc.
(dated) To take refreshment; to eat or drink.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: The periodic energizing required to maintain the contents of computer memory, the display luminance of a computer screen, etc.
The update of a display (in a web browser or similar software) to show the latest version of the data.
The process of modernizing something.

core.definition: To make someone feel more energetic or alert, or to reload a web page to show its latest content.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'FRESH', and the first syllable is a reduced 'rih'. The 'sh' ending should be crisp, not 'sh-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; refreshing is generally a compliment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'refresh' for both body and technology: 'I need to refresh' or 'Refresh the page'. The browser sense is everyday in offices. Calling someone 'refreshing' is a compliment about their honest, lively manner. In casual speech, 'Let me refresh your memory' is a polite way to restate a point.

distinctions.note: Renew implies restoring something to a valid or new state, such as a license; refresh suggests restoring energy or freshness.
Reload is the common technical term in software; refresh is more general and used by many web browsers.

examples.everyday: Let me refresh the page, because I think the tickets just came in.
examples.professional: Could you refresh the dashboard so we see yesterday's numbers before the meeting?
examples.analytical: The sermon sought to refresh the congregation's sense of God's presence without abandoning doctrinal clarity.

nuance.analogy: Refreshing is like opening a window in a stuffy room: the air changes right away.
nuance.etymology: From Old French refreschir, to make fresh again, from fresche, fresh.
common_mistakes: Saying 'refresh me' to mean 'refresh my memory'; Americans usually say 'refresh my memory'.
Confusing 'refresh' the verb with 'refreshment', which means food or drink.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word anapsyxis, meaning a cooling or refreshment, appears in Acts 3:20 in RSV, where Peter speaks of times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord. The related verb anapauō, to give rest or refresh, appears in Philemon 1:7, where Paul says the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through Philemon. Acts 3:19 in RSV calls for repentance so that times of refreshing may come from the Lord's presence, linking refreshment with repentance and restoration.

refresh.etymology: From Middle English *refreshen*, *refreschen*, *refrisschen*, from Old French *refrescher* (“to refresh”), equivalent to *re* + *fresh*.

core.definition: The son and successor of King Solomon, who ruled the southern kingdom of Judah after the kingdom of Israel split from it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -BOH-. The first 'e' is reduced to 'ih', and the final syllable is a light 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical and biblical name, sometimes used figuratively for a harsh or unwise leader.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know Rehoboam from Bible study and the story of the divided kingdom. In casual talk, people would say 'the son of Solomon' to avoid confusion. It is mostly used in religious or historical settings.

distinctions.note: Rehoboam was a king of Judah, while Rehob is a town or a different king in other passages.

examples.everyday: My friend says the story of Rehoboam is a good lesson about listening to good advice.
examples.professional: In the sermon I quoted the advice of the older counselors to Rehoboam about how to treat the people.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Rehoboam's reign in 1 Kings 12 presents the division of the kingdom as a consequence of his harsh reply to the people.

nuance.analogy: Like a leader whose one bad decision split a family business in two.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Rehav'am', meaning the people is enlarged or the kinsmen are enlarged.
common_mistakes: Confusing him with Jeroboam, who led the northern kingdom of Israel.
Mispronouncing the stress; the stress is on -BOH-.
nuance.biblical_note: Rehoboam was the son of Solomon and the first king of Judah after the kingdom split. The Hebrew name 'Rehav'am' combines a root meaning enlarge with a word for people. Key passages include 1 Kings 12, which describes his harsh reply to the people and the division of the kingdom, and 2 Chronicles 10, which gives a parallel account of the same events.

rehoboam.etymology: After Rehoboam, Judean king, the name of which in Biblical Hebrew was *רְחַבְעָם*

senses.definition: A machine-learning paradigm in which a model or agent learns by taking actions and receiving reward signals that indicate how well those actions achieve a desired objective.
Learning that occurs through reinforcement, especially through rewards, encouragement, or other consequences that strengthen desired behaviors.

core.definition: A machine-learning method in which an agent learns by taking actions and receiving rewards or penalties that show how well it is doing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'LEARN', and 'reinforcement' keeps only a secondary stress on '-FORCE-'. Do not pronounce the final 't' of 'reinforcement' strongly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term in computing and artificial intelligence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in computer science, data science and AI, especially when discussing games, robotics or recommendation systems. It is usually abbreviated as RL in technical writing. In casual conversation, people may say 'the AI learns by trial and error,' which is the everyday version of the idea.

distinctions.note: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples with correct answers; reinforcement learning learns from rewards or penalties after actions.
Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data; reinforcement learning is driven by a goal and feedback from the environment.

examples.everyday: My coworker is explaining how the robot vacuum learns its route, and he said it uses reinforcement learning.
examples.professional: We're testing reinforcement learning to optimize the pricing engine's daily decisions against revenue targets.
examples.analytical: Reinforcement learning formalizes learning as an agent's search for behavior that maximizes expected cumulative reward.

nuance.analogy: Like training a dog with treats: the animal learns which actions earn rewards.
nuance.etymology: Reinforcement comes from Old French renforcier; the machine-learning sense borrows the behaviorist term for reward-driven learning.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with supervised learning, which uses labeled correct answers rather than delayed rewards.
Stressing 'reinforcement' as the main stress of the phrase instead of 'LEARNING'.

conversation.text: In reinforcement learning, an agent learns a policy by trying actions and receiving rewards.
Reinforcement learning is hard to use here because we can't safely explore in production.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback is used to make chat models more helpful.

senses.definition: To transmit or send (e.g. money in payment); to supply.
To forgive, pardon (a wrong, offense, etc.).
To refrain from exacting or enforcing; to cancel.
senses.example: to remit the performance of an obligation

senses.definition: To allow (something) to slacken, to relax (one's attention etc.).
To refer (something or someone) for deliberation, judgment, etc. (to a particular body or person).
To restore or replace.
To postpone.
A communication from a superior court to a subordinate court.

core.definition: To send money to pay for something or to someone, especially a payment for goods or services.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MIT, as in 'permit' with a different first syllable. The noun 'REE-mit' stresses the first syllable, so don't mix them up.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a business or official word.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, remit most often appears in invoices, payment instructions, and letters: 'Please remit payment within 30 days.' In casual speech Americans say send, pay, or mail. The word is more common in writing than in speech.

distinctions.note: Send is everyday and general. Remit is formal and used specifically for paying money or submitting a payment.
Pardon is forgiving a person for a wrong. Remit as a verb in the sense of forgive is archaic; in modern usage its meaning is about sending money.

examples.everyday: I'll remit the rent to my landlord by check this week.
examples.professional: Please remit payment to the address on the invoice within thirty days.
examples.analytical: Under the contract, the buyer must remit the full amount before the goods are released.

nuance.analogy: Like a bank transfer that moves money from one account to another, sending it on its way.
nuance.etymology: From Latin remittere, meaning to send back or let go.
common_mistakes: Using remit with a preposition: say remit payment to someone, not remit to payment.
Saying remit in casual speech, where send or pay is more natural.

remit.etymology: From Middle English *remitten*, from Latin *remittō* (“to send, send back”).

senses.definition: Violent or otherwise punitive response to an act of harm or perceived injustice; a hitting back; revenge.

core.definition: A harmful or punishing response to someone who has harmed you, often done as revenge.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AY, the syllable before -shun. The earlier syllables are lighter, and the t in retal is a flap in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes hostile or punitive action, and in workplace contexts it can be legally serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use retaliation in legal and workplace settings, such as retaliation for filing a complaint, which is illegal in many cases. In everyday talk people might say payback or getting even. Americans say in retaliation for, not as a retaliation to something.

distinctions.note: Revenge is more personal and emotional, while retaliation can be an official or organized response to a particular harm.
Reprisal is often a military or political punishment imposed by one group on another, while retaliation can be personal or institutional.

examples.everyday: My landlord raised the rent in retaliation for us complaining about the broken heater.
examples.professional: HR reminded managers that any retaliation against someone who reports harassment is prohibited.
examples.analytical: Scholars distinguish between retaliation as proportional response and retaliation as an unbounded cycle of revenge.

nuance.analogy: Like a sharp echo that returns the same sound, only louder and harder.
nuance.etymology: From Latin talio, like-for-like, through retaliare, to repay in kind.
common_mistakes: Saying as a retaliation instead of in retaliation.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ree-tal-ee-AY-shun, which is fine, but dropping the final shun into shee-ən or sounding like shin.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or happening during run time.
senses.example: a run-time error

core.definition: The period during which a program is executing, or the environment in which a program runs.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, RUN, and the second part is a clear 'time' with a long 'i'. Do not reduce the second part to 'tum'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is used precisely in software, and has no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers and data scientists use this word when discussing code, containers and model deployment. As an adjective, 'runtime errors' are errors that occur while the program is running. Outside technical work, the word is rarely used, and people would say 'running time' for the length of a movie.
word_family: run time (noun, two words in general use)

distinctions.note: 'Compile time' is when code is translated into machine instructions, while 'runtime' is when the compiled program is actually executing.
'Running time' is the everyday term for the length of a movie or race; 'runtime' in software means the execution period.

examples.everyday: My laptop crashed with some kind of runtime error, so I restarted the app.
examples.professional: The model works in testing, but it fails at runtime when the input format changes.
examples.analytical: Type checking at compile time catches a different class of errors than checking at runtime.

nuance.analogy: Compile time is like writing a recipe, while runtime is the moment the cook actually follows it in the kitchen.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'run' and 'time'.
common_mistakes: Writing it as 'run time' when a software term is meant; the one-word form is standard in technical writing.
Confusing it with 'compile time', which happens earlier in the development process.

senses.definition: A local or state tax imposed as a percentage of the selling price of goods or services payable by the customer and collected by the seller for the local or state authorities.
A use tax or a combination of a sales tax and a use tax.
senses.example: They had to pay sales tax on a car they bought out of state.

core.definition: A tax added as a percentage to the price of goods or services, paid by the customer and collected by the seller for the government.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second word, tax, so the phrase has a strong beat on the end. The x is a /ks/ sound, and the s of sales is a /z/ sound, so it sounds like saylz TAKS.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a routine fact of American shopping, and people mention it when discussing prices.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, sales tax is set by each state, county and city, so rates vary; some states like Oregon and Delaware have none. Receipts usually show the tax as a separate line, and the price on the tag is often before tax. Americans commonly say 'Plus tax?' or 'Is that with tax?' when checking how much they will pay.

distinctions.note: VAT, value-added tax, is used in Europe and most other countries and is collected at each stage of production, while American sales tax is charged only once at the final sale.
Income tax is based on what you earn, while sales tax is based on what you spend.

examples.everyday: The shirt is twenty dollars, but with sales tax it comes to about twenty-one fifty.
examples.professional: Our finance team needs to confirm the sales tax rate for each shipping address before invoicing.
examples.analytical: Sales tax places the economic burden on consumers while the seller acts as a collection agent for the state.

nuance.analogy: Sales tax is like a small toll added at the checkout counter: you pay it every time you buy something, and the seller passes it along to the government.
nuance.etymology: Sales comes from Old English 'sala', and tax comes from Latin 'taxare', to assess or estimate.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sales taxes' when speaking generally; the normal phrase is 'sales tax' as a mass noun.
Pronouncing the final x as /s/ alone, when it is /ks/.

conversation.text: Is sales tax included in that price?
The sales tax here is about eight percent.
Oregon has no sales tax, so people drive there to shop.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or connected with satire.
senses.example: Spitting Image was a famous satirical television program.

core.definition: Using satire to mock or criticize people, institutions, or behavior, often through humor or exaggeration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TIH. The final -al is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'kul', and the middle r is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly critical; it describes a comic style that targets someone, often with a sharp edge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use satirical in everyday speech and writing, for example about a newspaper column, a TV sketch, or a funny political cartoon. It is the most common adjective in this family. Saying something is satirical implies it is meant as a critique, so it is a good way to explain why a joke is not literal.

distinctions.note: Satirical is more common and natural in spoken American English, while satiric sounds more technical.
Ironic describes a contrast between expectation and outcome, while satirical describes a work that mocks a target on purpose.

examples.everyday: Did you read that satirical article about the city council? It's so funny because it's true.
examples.professional: The team's satirical slide deck about our meeting schedule got a big laugh, but it made the point clearly.
examples.analytical: The novel's satirical portrait of academic life exposes the vanity of scholars who value status over truth.

nuance.analogy: A satirical piece is like a caricature: it exaggerates the real features of its subject to show what is wrong with them.
nuance.etymology: From satire, from Latin satura, meaning medley.
common_mistakes: Using satirical to mean sarcastic in a personal, spoken way; satire is usually aimed at a broader target.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: A mindset, skill, or type of behavior so ingrained through habit or practice that it seems natural, automatic, or without a basis in conscious thought.

core.definition: A habit or skill that has become so ingrained through practice that you do it automatically, without thinking about it.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on NAY in 'nature', and 'second' is a light, secondary stress; the d in 'second' is often dropped in fast speech, so it sounds like SEK-un. The -ture ending is pronounced CHUR in American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually praises a skill or habit that has become effortless, though it can describe an unwelcome habit too.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase freely in conversation and at work, for example 'Public speaking is second nature to her'. It works with 'to' followed by a noun or a verb ing-form. A natural reply is 'Yeah, you get used to it' or simply a nod.

distinctions.note: A habit is any regular behavior, while second nature stresses that the behavior has become automatic, almost instinctive.
An instinct is inborn, whereas second nature is learned through repetition and practice.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about the stick shift; driving it will be second nature after a week.
examples.professional: Running the deployment pipeline is second nature to the team now, so we can focus on the new features.
examples.analytical: For Aristotle, virtue becomes a kind of second nature through repeated action, which is why habituation matters so much.

nuance.analogy: Like walking downstairs in the dark: you no longer think about each step because your body has learned the pattern.
nuance.etymology: 'Second nature' appears in English from the 1500s, with 'second' meaning 'following' in contrast with a person's inborn first nature.
common_mistakes: Saying 'It is second nature for me' instead of 'to me'; the correct preposition is to.
Using it for a single one-time action; it describes a habit built by repetition.

conversation.text: After a few months, driving on the left became second nature.
For her, writing SQL is second nature.
Once you practice, saying no politely becomes second nature.

senses.definition: Organized incitement of rebellion or civil disorder against authority or the state, usually by speech or writing.
Insurrection or rebellion.

core.definition: Organized speech or writing that urges people to rebel against the government or public authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable DISH. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final syllable is a reduced 'un' sound, not a full 'on'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; implies a serious threat to public order and is often used by authorities to condemn critics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sedition mainly in legal, political and historical contexts, such as court cases or discussions of the Sedition Act of 1798. It is a strong charge, so calling someone seditious in ordinary conversation sounds heavy and political. In daily life people more often say 'treason' or 'inciting violence' when they mean something similar.

distinctions.note: Treason is betrayal of one's own country, often defined in law as making war against it or aiding its enemies, while sedition is inciting others to rebel without necessarily taking action.
Rebellion is the armed or open revolt itself, while sedition is the incitement or agitation that encourages it.

examples.everyday: My uncle says that talk on the radio is basically sedition, but I think he's exaggerating.
examples.professional: Legal counsel told the communications team that the draft post could be read as sedition, so we removed the language before it went public.
examples.analytical: The line between political dissent and sedition depends on whether speech merely criticizes authority or deliberately urges its violent overthrow.

nuance.analogy: Like a match thrown into dry grass: the words themselves may be small, but they can start a fire.
nuance.etymology: From Latin seditio, 'a going apart, discord, mutiny', from sed- 'apart' and itio 'going'.
common_mistakes: Confusing sedition with sedation, which is a medical term for calming drugs.
Using sedition for any protest; it specifically means urging rebellion or disorder against authority.

sedition.etymology: From Old French *sedicion*, from Latin *sēditiō* (“sedition, discord”), from *sēd-* (“apart”) (an alternative form of *sē-*) + *itiō* (“going”).

senses.definition: Attractive; alluring; tempting.
senses.example: Evil is said to be seductive, which is one reason why people do what they know they shouldn't.

core.definition: Very attractive or appealing in a way that tempts you to want or do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DUK, and the first vowel is a reduced sound like 'ih'. The final syllable is a short 'iv', not 'eev'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; can be playful for food or ideas, but suggests sexual allure or temptation when describing people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seductive for appealing things like a smell, a deal or a plan, and also for sexual attraction. Describing a person as seductive can sound flirtatious or inappropriate at work. For food and ideas, it is a lively way to say something is very tempting.

distinctions.note: Attractive is the general and neutral word for appealing, while seductive suggests a strong, sometimes risky pull.
Tempting usually refers to something you want, while seductive adds a sense of being drawn in, often beyond your better judgment.

examples.everyday: That smell from the bakery is seductive, I can't walk past without buying something.
examples.professional: The vendor's pricing looks seductive, but we should check the hidden fees before we sign anything.
examples.analytical: Simple explanations are seductive because they relieve the discomfort of uncertainty, yet they often conceal the real complexity.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm porch light on a cold night that pulls you toward it.
nuance.etymology: From seduce, from Latin seducere 'to lead aside'.
common_mistakes: Using seductive for a person in a work setting, which can sound inappropriate.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'sih-DOOK-tiv'.

senses.definition: A pause or rest of a contemplative nature.

A word occurring between verses or paragraphs in parts of the Hebrew Bible, namely in Habakkuk and the Psalms; perhaps indicating a pause, either for contemplation or for clearing the throat in singing.

core.definition: A Hebrew word in the Psalms and Habakkuk, probably marking a pause in the music or reading for reflection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, like the end of 'sofa'. Do not say 'sell-ah' with a short e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly know selah from the Psalms in Bible reading, sermons and worship songs. In church, it is often read silently or sung as a pause for reflection. It is rarely used in ordinary conversation, and saying it casually may sound like a religious reference.

distinctions.note: Amen is a response of agreement or closing affirmation, while selah marks a pause within the text itself.
Pause is a general English word; selah is a specific liturgical or scriptural marker with uncertain meaning.

examples.everyday: At Bible study, the leader said selah after the verse, so we all paused for a moment.
examples.professional: In my sermon on Psalm 46, I explained that selah likely marks a musical pause for the congregation to reflect.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether selah indicates a musical interlude, a liturgical response or a rhetorical break in the Psalter.

nuance.analogy: Selah is like a rest mark in sheet music: the reader stops, lets the words settle, and then continues.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew selah, of uncertain meaning, possibly from a root meaning 'to lift up' or 'to pause'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'SELL-uh' with a short e, as in 'self'.
Treating selah as a word that means 'amen' or a closing blessing.
nuance.biblical_note: Selah (Hebrew selah) is a term of uncertain meaning that appears 71 times in the Psalms and 3 times in Habakkuk. Most scholars think it marks a pause, a musical interlude or a moment of reflection. Psalm 3:2 places it after a verse about many saying God will not help the psalmist, showing a pause for reflection. Habakkuk 3:3 places it after a line describing God's glory, inviting the reader to stop and consider it. Psalm 46:3 and 46:7 use it after verses about God as a refuge, pausing to reflect on his power.

senses.definition: An act or process of referring to itself or oneself.
(uncommon) To reference itself or oneself.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: The act of a statement, object or process referring back to itself or to its own author.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on REF, the first syllable of reference, and the second syllable is reduced to a weak er sound. Do not pronounce the final -ence as 'ance'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term in logic and computing, and it can sound playful when used of jokes or media.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use self-reference mostly in logic, mathematics, computer science and literary criticism. In everyday talk people more often say that a joke or show is self-referential, or that someone is talking about themselves, but they usually choose words like self-reflection or self-absorption for the personal sense. The noun is typically used without an article in general statements, such as 'self-reference can cause paradoxes'.

distinctions.note: Self-reflection is thinking about one's own thoughts and behavior, usually in a personal way, while self-reference is about a statement or system pointing back to itself.
Recursion is a process defined in terms of itself, usually calling itself on smaller inputs, while self-reference is a broader idea that also covers sentences and texts.

examples.everyday: That sitcom has a lot of self-reference, with characters joking about being on television.
examples.professional: The compiler flagged the function because its self-reference never reaches a base case.
examples.analytical: Godel's construction depends on a carefully engineered self-reference that lets a formula talk about its own provability.

nuance.analogy: Like a mirror that shows a picture of itself, a self-reference points back at the thing that contains it.
nuance.etymology: From self plus reference, which comes from Latin referre, to carry back.
common_mistakes: Writing 'self reference' without a hyphen in formal writing, where the hyphen is expected.
Using it for ordinary thinking about oneself, where self-reflection is the more natural word.

senses.definition: Describes models that map an input sequence to an output sequence, as in translation.

core.definition: Describes a machine learning model that maps an input sequence, such as a sentence, to an output sequence, such as its translation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress both first syllables, SEE, and reduce to in the middle, so it sounds like 'SEE-kwuns-tuh-SEE-kwuns' in fast speech. The final syllable is a soft -uns.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a precise technical term used in artificial intelligence.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers and researchers use this phrase in papers, design reviews and team discussions about translation, summarization and speech systems. It is almost always used as an adjective before a noun, such as a sequence-to-sequence model. Outside AI, people would not understand it without explanation.

distinctions.note: A transformer is an architecture that can be used for sequence-to-sequence tasks, while sequence-to-sequence describes the task of mapping one sequence to another.
Classification assigns a single label to an input, while sequence-to-sequence produces a whole output sequence.

examples.everyday: Our translation app uses a sequence-to-sequence model, so it reads the whole sentence before writing the translation.
examples.professional: In the design review, we agreed to use a sequence-to-sequence model for the summarization feature.
examples.analytical: A sequence-to-sequence model separates encoding the input from decoding the output, which raises questions about how information is compressed between the two stages.

nuance.analogy: Like a simultaneous interpreter who listens to a whole sentence, understands it, and then speaks the translation.
nuance.etymology: Compound of sequence and to, used in machine learning research from the 2010s.
common_mistakes: Stressing only the first word and making the phrase sound like one word.
Using the phrase for any AI model; it specifically refers to input and output sequences.
Saying 'sequence to sequence' without hyphens in formal writing, which can create confusion in technical documents.

conversation.text: A sequence-to-sequence model maps one sequence to another, like a sentence in English to one in French.
Summarization fits naturally into a sequence-to-sequence setup.

senses.definition: Similar in appearance or texture (especially in softness and smoothness) to silk.
senses.example: silky hair

senses.definition: Smooth and pleasant; seductive.
senses.example: a silky voice

senses.definition: Having sensibilities of mainstream culture, in contrast to crunchy.
senses.example: Cribs and formula, strollers and baby food epitomize silky parenting.

senses.definition: Covered in long, slender, glistening hairs pressed close to the surface; sericeous.

core.definition: Smooth, soft, and fine in texture, like silk.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final y is pronounced as a long ee sound, and the i in the first syllable is short, as in sit.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests smoothness and luxury, especially for fabric, hair, and food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use silky about fabric, hair, skin, sauces, and desserts to praise a smooth feel. It can also describe a smooth, polished voice or manner, sometimes with a slightly suspicious tone. In food, silky often describes a smooth, creamy texture, as in a silky custard.

distinctions.note: Smooth describes any even surface; silky suggests a softer, finer, more luxurious feel.
Velvety describes a soft, thick texture with a short nap; silky describes a fine, slippery feel.

examples.everyday: This pasta sauce is so silky, you have to try a bite.
examples.professional: The client liked the silky finish of the new interface.
examples.analytical: His silky rhetoric gave his argument a charm that concealed its weakness.

nuance.analogy: Like a smooth river surface that reflects light without a ripple.
nuance.etymology: From silk, with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using silky for hard or rough surfaces by mistake.
Pronouncing the i like the ee in see.

conversation.text: The custard was silky and smooth.
Add butter to make the sauce silky.
This tofu has a silky texture.

senses.definition: Something that simulates a system or environment in order to predict actual behavior.
senses.example: This exercise is a simulation of actual battle conditions.

senses.definition: The process of simulating.
senses.example: Despite extensive simulation in the design phase, the aircraft failed to behave as expected.

senses.definition: A video game designed to convey a more or less realistic experience, as of a sport or warfare.
senses.example: Some kids in the classroom will be playing simulations after school.

senses.definition: Assuming an appearance which is feigned, or not true.
The act of falling over in order to be awarded a foul, when no foul has been committed.

core.definition: A computer or physical model that imitates a real system or environment to predict how it will behave.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAY. The ending -tion is pronounced 'shun', and the final syllable has no separate vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday talk it can mean a video game or a training exercise, and in technical talk it means a computed model.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use simulation for flight training, Monte Carlo runs and racing games. In data and engineering work, a simulation is a run of a model over many scenarios. In casual conversation, people often use it for a driving or racing video game.

distinctions.note: A model is the mathematical or physical structure; a simulation is running that model over time to see what happens.
Emulation copies the behavior of another system, often on different hardware; simulation predicts the behavior of a real-world system.
A prediction is a single expected outcome; a simulation is a tool that generates many possible outcomes.

examples.everyday: My son spends hours on a racing simulation game.
examples.professional: Let's run a simulation of the new pricing model before we commit to it.
examples.analytical: A simulation can reproduce a pattern without explaining why it occurs, which is a real limit of the method.

nuance.analogy: A simulation is like a wind tunnel for ideas: you test a design against imagined weather before you build it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin simulatio, from simulare, to imitate.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as SIM-yoo-lay-shun.
Using simulation for a video game in professional writing without context; in data work it means a computed model.

simulation.etymology: First attested in 1340 as Middle English *symulacioun*, from Middle French *simulation*, from Old French *simulation*/*simulacion*, from Latin *simulātiōnem*, from *simulō* (“imitate”).

conversation.text: Training in simulation is cheap and safe, but the robot still has to work in the real world.
We built a simulation of the support desk so the agent can practice on synthetic customers.
The flight simulation felt surprisingly real.

core.definition: The mountain in the Sinai wilderness where God gave Moses the Law and made the covenant with Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SY, and the final -ai is pronounced 'eye'. Avoid saying it as sin-AY or sigh-NAY.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a place name, though it carries strong religious significance in Judaism and Christianity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Sinai in Bible study, history and news about Egypt. Mount Sinai names the mountain, while the Sinai Peninsula names the region in Egypt. In theology, phrases like the Sinai covenant are common.

distinctions.note: Horeb is another name for the mountain of the Law in Deuteronomy; Sinai is the usual name in Exodus.
The Sinai Peninsula is a modern region of Egypt, while Mount Sinai is a specific mountain within the biblical story.

collocations: the Ten Commandments given at Sinai

examples.everyday: We visited a church named after Mount Sinai when we went to Egypt.
examples.professional: The sermon series connected the Exodus narrative with the covenant given at Sinai.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the traditional site of Sinai in the southern peninsula is the original location of the covenant.

nuance.analogy: Sinai is like the place where the rules of a nation were first written down and signed.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; no firm etymology is established.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in sigh-NAY.
Confusing Mount Sinai with the Sinai Peninsula, which is a larger region in Egypt.
nuance.biblical_note: Sinai is where Moses received the Law. Exodus 19 describes God descending on the mountain, and Exodus 20 gives the Ten Commandments. Exodus 34:29 describes Moses coming down from the mountain with his face shining after speaking with God. Galatians 4:24-25 uses Mount Sinai allegorically, linking it with the covenant of bondage.

senses.definition: A measure of the asymmetry of the probability distribution of a real-valued random variable; is the third standardized moment, defined as γ1=μ3σ3, where μ3 is the third moment about the mean and σ is the standard deviation.
The property of being skew.

core.definition: A measure of how asymmetric a probability distribution is; positive skew means a longer right tail, negative skew a longer left tail.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ew' in 'skew' is a long oo sound, so say SKYOO, not SKOO. The final -ness is a reduced, unstressed 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in statistics, data science and quantitative research, where it is a precise technical term. Analysts often say 'the data is right-skewed' or 'skewness is positive' when describing a distribution. Outside technical settings, Americans would say 'lopsidedness' or 'asymmetry' instead.

distinctions.note: Skewness measures asymmetry (lean left or right), while kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are and how peaked the distribution is.
Asymmetry is the general idea of lacking symmetry; skewness is the specific third-moment measure of it for a distribution.

examples.everyday: My commute times are really skewed by a few terrible days when the highway closes.
examples.professional: The revenue data has strong positive skewness, so I'll use the median instead of the mean in the dashboard.
examples.analytical: A distribution with zero skewness is symmetric about its mean, though zero skewness alone does not guarantee a normal distribution.

nuance.analogy: Skewness is like a mountain range that leans to one side: the slope is gentle on one side and steep on the other.
nuance.etymology: From 'skew', probably from Old Norse or Middle English roots meaning oblique or slanting, with the -ness noun suffix added.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ew' as a short vowel, as in 'skuh-NESS'.
Confusing skewness with kurtosis, which is a different shape measure.

senses.definition: Any of various concave objects (or portions of larger objects) that envelop a counterpart object.
An opening into which a plug or other connecting part is designed to fit (e.g. a light bulb socket).
The socket head for a socket wrench.
A hollow tool for grasping and lifting tools dropped in a well-boring.
The hollow of a candlestick.
One endpoint of a two-way communication link, used for interprocess communication across a network.
One endpoint of a two-way named pipe on Unix and Unix-like systems, used for interprocess communication.
A steel apparatus attached to a saddle to protect the thighs and legs.
The vagina.
A hollow into a bone which a part fits, such as an eye, or another bone, in the case of a joint.
To place or fit in a socket.

core.definition: A hole or device in a wall, fixture or appliance into which a plug or light bulb is inserted to make an electrical connection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAH, and say the second vowel as a short, reduced 'ih'. Do not add an extra syllable, and remember the t is quiet-ish and not flapped in this position.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for household and technical objects.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use socket for electrical outlets in the sense of a fitting for a bulb, and also for the sockets on tools and machines.
